sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and vocabulary (Theme 1: Activities at home and school)
learning_experiences: listen to an oral text with words containing the target-letter sound combinations as modelled by peers, teacher, or from audio recording,
point out words with the target sound combinations from the text,
watch videos on conveyoursations with words featuring the target letter- sounds: (bl, br, cl and sound /tʃ/),
take turns to practise saying words with the target letter-sound combinations,
play word games with peers involving target sounds,
work jointly to match new words with their meaning,
use new words to construct sentences with peers and give feedback to each other,
create a talking tree using the vocabulary learnt.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we pronounce words correctly?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication: The learner’s ability to listen keenly and actively is enhanced as they listen to oral texts and recognise words with the target letter-sound combinations.
Creativity and imagination: This is nurtured as the learner embraces ideas that inspire creativity when creating a talking tree using the vocabulary learnt.
sub_strands.values: Respect is enhanced as the learner appreciates the effort of peers when working jointly to match new words with their meaning.
sub_strands.pcis: Environmental awareness: This is promoted as the learner familiarises with activities at home and school.
sub_strands.links: The learner can relate the concept of correct pronunciation to learning of similar concepts in Kiswahili and Indigenous Language Activities.

skills.name: Hear and pick out words with bl, br, cl and ch
skills.mastery: The child hears and picks out words with bl, br, cl and the sound /tʃ/ (ch) in a sentence or short oral text (for example blue, brush, clap, chair) and tells them from words that differ by one sound. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: circle the words with the sound

prerequisites.reason: Grade 2 told apart words with bl, sp, sc, sk and ck. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 2 recognised /tʃ/ and /kl/. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Say words that begin with two or three consonants together
skills.mastery: The child says words that start with a consonant blend (bl, br, cl, dr, fl, fr, gl, cr, pl, st, sn, pr, sm, sw, sp, thr, gr, shr, spl, spr, str, scr) as one beat, with no vowel slipped between the consonants and no consonant dropped. Evidence rule: the teacher hears it done right on two different days, scored with the observation rubric (PLAN_OBSERVATION_RUBRICS.md); a tapped answer cannot show it.
question_forms: say the word after the teacher

Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

misconceptions.error: Hears bl and br as the same sound.

example.question: Which word starts with bl: blue, brown, clap?

misconceptions.cause: Several Kenyan home languages do not keep /l/ and /r/ apart, so bl and br sound alike.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "brown" beside "blue" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Watch the tongue: up behind the teeth for l, curled back for r.
misconceptions.feedback: Watch the tongue: up behind the teeth for l, curled back for r.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Picks any word that starts with the first letter of the blend.

example.question: Which word starts with bl: bag, black, cup?

misconceptions.cause: The child listens for the first letter only, not the two sounds together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "bag" beside "black" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Say it slowly: b-l-ack. Bag has b, then a.
misconceptions.feedback: Say it slowly: b-l-ack. Bag has b, then a.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Hears ch (/tʃ/) as sh (/ʃ/).

example.question: Which word starts with the sound in chair: shop, chin, sun?

misconceptions.cause: A home language with sh and no ch (or the reverse) carries over.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "shop" beside "chin" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Ch starts with a stop, like a sneeze: t-sh, chin.
misconceptions.feedback: Ch starts with a stop, like a sneeze: t-sh, chin.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Hears a vowel between the two consonants and claps two beats.

example.question: Clap the beats in "clap".

misconceptions.cause: Bantu languages build syllables that end in a vowel, so a vowel is heard in English clusters.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "2 (ku-lap)" beside "1" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: C and l are glued together: one clap, clap.
misconceptions.feedback: C and l are glued together: one clap, clap.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Slips a vowel between the consonants of a blend.

example.question: Say: blue

misconceptions.cause: Bantu languages build syllables that end in a vowel.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "bulu" beside "blue" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Glue the two consonants: b-l, blue, one beat.
misconceptions.feedback: Glue the two consonants: b-l, blue, one beat.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Says l for r, or r for l, in a blend.

example.question: Say: The frog can fly.

misconceptions.cause: L and r are one sound in some home languages.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The flog can fry." beside "The frog can fly." in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Tongue up for l, curled back for r.
misconceptions.feedback: Tongue up for l, curled back for r.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Drops one consonant of the blend.

example.question: Say: stop

misconceptions.cause: Two consonants together feel hard, so one is left out.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "top" beside "stop" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Start with the hiss, then t: sss-top.
misconceptions.feedback: Start with the hiss, then t: sss-top.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Says thr as tr.

example.question: Say: three

misconceptions.cause: Th is missing in most Kenyan home languages.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "tree" beside "three" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Tongue between the teeth, blow, then r.
misconceptions.feedback: Tongue between the teeth, blow, then r.

misconceptions.error: Uses a thing word for a person word.

example.question: A person who cooks food in a hotel is a ...

misconceptions.cause: Common Kenyan English: cooker is the stove, not the person.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "cooker" beside "cook" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: A cook is a person; a cooker is the stove.
misconceptions.feedback: A cook is a person; a cooker is the stove.

example.question: The animal that gives us wool is a ...

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "goat" beside "sheep" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Think about what makes this one different: wool comes from sheep.
misconceptions.feedback: Think about what makes this one different: wool comes from sheep.

example.question: We wear a ... on our head when riding a bicycle.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "hammer" beside "helmet" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Say the sentence with the word: does it make sense?
misconceptions.feedback: Say the sentence with the word: does it make sense?

skills.name: Read a Grade 3 text aloud accurately and at the right speed
skills.mastery: The child reads a short Grade 3 text aloud with almost every word right, sounding out unfamiliar words with the letter-sound combinations learnt instead of guessing, at a steady speed (about 60 to 80 words a minute is a guide, to confirm by the teacher). Evidence rule: the teacher hears it done right on two different days, scored with the observation rubric (PLAN_OBSERVATION_RUBRICS.md); a tapped answer cannot show it.
question_forms: read a page of a graded reader
timed reading of a short passage

misconceptions.error: Guesses a word from its first letter or the picture.

example.question: Read: The cow is in the house.
example.wrong_answer: The cow is in the horse.
example.correct_answer: The cow is in the house.

misconceptions.cause: Sight-word guessing: the child has learnt to guess from the first letter and the picture instead of reading every letter.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The cow is in the horse." beside "The cow is in the house." in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Look at every letter, left to right: h-ou-se.
misconceptions.feedback: Look at every letter, left to right: h-ou-se.

misconceptions.error: Reads b as d or d as b.

example.question: Read: The bed is big.

misconceptions.cause: B and d are the same shape turned round, and young readers often still mix them.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The deb is dig." beside "The bed is big." in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Make a bed with your fists: b first (left), d last (right).
misconceptions.feedback: Make a bed with your fists: b first (left), d last (right).

misconceptions.error: Skips small words such as the, a and of.

example.question: Read: A cup of tea is on the table.
example.correct_answer: A cup of tea is on the table.

misconceptions.cause: Small words carry little meaning for the child and the eye jumps to the big ones.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Cup tea is on table." beside "A cup of tea is on the table." in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Point under every word as you read it.
misconceptions.feedback: Point under every word as you read it.

misconceptions.error: Reads word by word with a stop after each word.

example.question: Read: Wanjiru sweeps the classroom every morning.
example.wrong_answer: Wanjiru. Sweeps. The. Classroom. Every. Morning.
example.correct_answer: Wanjiru sweeps the classroom / every morning.

misconceptions.cause: Each word is decoded on its own and not yet joined into phrases.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Wanjiru. Sweeps. The. Classroom. Every. Morning." beside "Wanjiru sweeps the classroom / every morning." in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Read it once in your head, then read it in two scoops.

sub_strands.sub_strand: Comprehension (Theme 1: Activities at home and school)
learning_experiences: look at pictures and titles of a text and predict the likely order of events in a story, with peers,
read a print or digital text, related to the theme,
identify the characters in a text,
draw a concept map to outline the characters in the text,
discuss the setting in a story, with peers,
respond to direct questions by locating sentences with the answers,
answer indirect questions using prior knowledge of the target theme,
list keywords or phrases related to the theme from a grade-appropriate text,
work jointly to use contextual clues to find meaning of the new words.
key_inquiry_questions: How can we tell how a story, poem, or conversation will end?
Why is it important to identify the main idea in a text?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and imagination: The learner’s ability to embrace new ideas in nurtured as they draw a concept map to outline the characters in the text.

sub_strands.values: Respect is enhanced as the learner appreciates diverse opinions from peers during discussions.
sub_strands.pcis: Social cohesion: This is enhanced as the learner interacts with texts on activities t home and in school and how they can take part in constructive activities.

Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

misconceptions.error: Describes the picture instead of predicting.

example.question: Title: The Lost Calf. Picture: a boy looking behind a bush. What will happen?
example.wrong_answer: There is a boy and a bush.
example.correct_answer: The boy will find the calf behind the bush.

misconceptions.cause: The child answers what is seen, not what will happen.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "There is a boy and a bush." beside "The boy will find the calf behind the bush." in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Ask: what will happen next? Use will.
misconceptions.feedback: Ask: what will happen next? Use will.

misconceptions.error: Makes a prediction with no link to the clues.

example.question: Title: The Big Race. What might the story be about?

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a wedding" beside "children running a race" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.

misconceptions.error: Gives something that has already happened.

example.question: Juma climbed the tree to get his kite. What will happen next?

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Juma climbed the tree." beside "He will get the kite and climb down." in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Next means after what we have read.

misconceptions.error: Will not predict because the guess might be wrong.

misconceptions.help: Good readers guess, then check.

skills.name: Answer questions whose answers are not stated but shown by clues
skills.mastery: The child answers why and how questions by joining clues in the text (She sat alone and cried: she was sad) and can point to the clue, without making up what the clues do not show. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Finding what is stated comes before joining clues. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 2 answered indirect questions. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Says the answer is not in the story when it is shown by clues.

example.question: Akinyi sat alone and cried when her goat got lost. How did she feel?

misconceptions.cause: The child looks only for the exact words.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It does not say." beside "sad" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: The writer shows, not tells: crying shows sad.
misconceptions.feedback: The writer shows, not tells: crying shows sad.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Picks a feeling word without using the clue.

example.question: Baraka jumped up and down when he won the race. How did he feel?

misconceptions.cause: A feeling is chosen from the child's own idea.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "tired" beside "happy" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: What does jumping up and down show?
misconceptions.feedback: What does jumping up and down show?
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Makes an answer the clues do not support.

example.question: The sky turned dark and the wind blew hard. What will happen soon?

misconceptions.cause: The child goes beyond the clues.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "There will be an earthquake." beside "It will rain." in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Use only what the clues show.
misconceptions.feedback: Use only what the clues show.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Mama took an umbrella." beside "because it looked like it would rain" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.

sub_strands.sub_strand: Forms of the verb ‘to do’ Subject- verb agreement (Theme 2: Sharing duties and responsibilities)
learning_experiences: listen for the forms of the verb ‘to do’ (do, does and did) from an audio recording/video clip or as modelled by the peers or the teacher,
construct sentences related to the theme using the different forms of the verb ‘to do’ (do, does and did) for subject-verb agreement. For example;

type sentences formed using the different forms of the verb ‘to do’ (do, does and did) onto a digital device in pairs,
play a language game with peers and use the different forms of the verb ‘to do’ (do, does and did) in their interactions.
key_inquiry_questions: What duties do you like doing?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and imagination: This is enhanced as the learner embraces ideas that inspire creativity when recite poems/sing songs about the theme, while using the different forms of the verb ‘to do’ (do, does and did).

sub_strands.values: Unity: Cooperation is enhanced as the learner collaborates with peers when playing language games.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills (Self-esteem): The learner’s self-esteem is improved through the use of the various forms of the verb ‘to do’ correctly in communication.
sub_strands.links: The learner can apply the knowledge acquired on the different forms of the verb ‘to do’ in learning of similar concepts in Kiswahili and Indigenous Languages Activities.

outcomes.text: identify the forms of the verb ‘to do’ (do, does and did) in a text

skills.name: Use do, does and did to agree with the subject
skills.mastery: The child picks do, does and did from a text and uses does with he, she and it, do with I, you, we and they, and did for the past, with a plain verb after it: Did you wash? She does her duties. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Agreeing a verb with its subject. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 2 used do, does and did. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses do with he, she or it.

example.question: Juma ... his homework every day.

misconceptions.cause: The -es on does is not heard as part of the rule for he and she.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "do" beside "does" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: He, she, it: does.
misconceptions.feedback: He, she, it: does.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Puts a past verb after did.

example.question: Did you ... the dishes? (wash)

misconceptions.cause: Did shows the past, and the child shows it again on the verb.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "washed" beside "wash" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Did already says past: the verb stays plain.
misconceptions.feedback: Did already says past: the verb stays plain.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Uses does or do for the past.

example.question: Last week she ... the cleaning.

misconceptions.cause: The present form is used for all times.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "does" beside "did" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Last week: did.
misconceptions.feedback: Last week: did.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

misconceptions.error: Uses does with I or you.

example.question: I ... my duties after school.

misconceptions.cause: Does is over-used once learnt.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "does" beside "do" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: I and you: do.
misconceptions.feedback: I and you: do.

skills.name: Leave a finger space between words and none inside a word
skills.mastery: The child leaves a finger space between words, no space inside a word, and spots writing where words run together or are split. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 2 recognised aspects of good handwriting. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Seeing letters as parts of words. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Runs words together with no space.

example.question: Which sentence is spaced right?

misconceptions.cause: Speech has no gaps, and the child writes as he or she hears.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Wesharetheduties." beside "We share the duties." in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Put a finger after each word.
misconceptions.feedback: Put a finger after each word.

misconceptions.error: Puts a space inside a word.

example.question: Which is right: "class room work" or "classroom work"?

misconceptions.cause: Long words are split where the child pauses.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "class room work" beside "classroom work" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: A word is one block: no gap inside.
misconceptions.feedback: A word is one block: no gap inside.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study

example.question: Which writing is easiest to read?

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "We      share      duties" beside "We share duties" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: One finger, no more.
misconceptions.feedback: One finger, no more.

example.question: How many words: "Mama cooks food."

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "4" beside "3" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.

misconceptions.feedback: Count the gaps, then add one.

skills.name: Hear and pick out words with cr, pl, st and sn

Grade 2 recognised cr. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Hears pl as bl (p and b swapped).

example.question: Which word starts with pl: plate, blade, slate?

misconceptions.cause: P and b are not kept apart by some speakers.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "blade" beside "plate" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Hold paper in front of your lips: p puffs, b does not.
misconceptions.feedback: Hold paper in front of your lips: p puffs, b does not.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "clown" beside "crown" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Curl the tongue back for crown.
misconceptions.feedback: Curl the tongue back for crown.

misconceptions.error: Swaps sn and sm.

example.question: Which word starts with sn: smell, snake, sun?

misconceptions.cause: N and m are both nose sounds and sound alike after s.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "smell" beside "snake" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: For sn the lips stay open; for sm they close.
misconceptions.feedback: For sn the lips stay open; for sm they close.

misconceptions.cause: A vowel is slipped in after s, as the home language does.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "2 (si-tone)" beside "1" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Ssss-t: hiss straight into t, one clap.
misconceptions.feedback: Ssss-t: hiss straight into t, one clap.

skills.name: Say what a text is mainly about and why it was written
skills.mastery: The child chooses the idea the whole text is about (how to keep the classroom clean), not one detail and not something too wide (school), and says whether the text tells a story, gives facts or tells us how to do something. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: what is the text mainly about

prerequisites.reason: Grade 2 identified the main idea, topic or purpose. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Knowing what the text says. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Summarise a short text in two or three sentences
skills.mastery: The child gives the main happenings in order in two or three short sentences, leaving out small details and his or her own opinion. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which sentence should be in the summary

prerequisites.reason: Knowing what matters most. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Keeping the events in order. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Put the events of a text in the order they happened
skills.mastery: The child puts three to five events in the order they happened, using first, then, after that and finally, and reads before and after correctly even when the text tells them out of order. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 2 retold events in sequence. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Finding each event in the text. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses a detail instead of the main idea.

example.question: A text about the ways children help at home: sweeping, washing dishes, feeding hens. What is it mainly about?

misconceptions.cause: One detail is remembered best.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "feeding hens" beside "how children help at home" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Which answer covers every part of the text?
misconceptions.feedback: Which answer covers every part of the text?

misconceptions.error: Chooses an idea that is too wide.

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "animals" beside "caring for a dog" in a fresh sentence or text and ask again; picking it again shows the error is still there.
misconceptions.help: Is the whole text about that, or a bit of it?
misconceptions.feedback: Is the whole text about that, or a bit of it?

misconceptions.help: Read it all, then decide.
misconceptions.feedback: Read it all, then decide.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: a common classroom error of Kenyan learners of English, written offline (18 Nov 2026), not traced to a study
